# Conclusion

In this thesis, I studied reject inference as a dynamic selective-observation
problem. The literature review showed that RI methods generally require
additional identifying assumptions or information beyond the observed outcomes
of accepted applicants and their covariates. This motivated a more explicit
formulation of the RI problem in which the acceptance mechanism is part of the
data-generating process rather than a static source of missingness. The
measure-theoretic formulation makes the role of the acceptance policy, the
observed and hidden variables, and the temporal feedback between successive
rounds explicit, avoiding having hidden assumptions as it was often found in
the literature review.

Based on this formulation, I developed a simulation framework in which the
applicant population remains stationary while the acceptance policy is
re-estimated from previously accepted applicants. This isolates the feedback
generated by selective observation from exogenous population drift. Within this
framework, I formulated and heuristically justified the hypothesis that acceptance
bias can become observable through changes in the accepted population and through
differences between historically estimated and subsequently realized model performance.

The numerical analysis provides evidence for the hypothesized overfocusing
mechanism. In the accepts-only policy, the acceptance threshold declines over
successive rounds and the acceptance rate correspondingly contracts, even
though the underlying applicant population is unchanged. The accepted
population therefore becomes increasingly concentrated in a region associated
with lower predicted default risk. This behavior is observed under both MAR
and the considered MNAR configurations and is consistent with a self-reinforcing
selection mechanism.

The analysis of the LR parameters provides a second perspective on the same
effect. The estimates obtained from the accepts of the full-information policy stabilize
quickly, whereas the accepts-only estimates can remain substantially farther
from the full-information parameters even when their training samples become
large. Under MNAR, some configurations additionally produce persistent
deviations from the full-information benchmark. These results should not be
interpreted as a proof that the LR estimators cease to be consistent: the
simulation is finite and does not establish their asymptotic behavior. They do,
however, show that increasing the number of accepted observations alone is not
sufficient to eliminate the discrepancy generated by the evolving acceptance
process in the simulated setting, at least given the sample sizes studied in this
simulation study.

The third part of the analysis investigated *surprise* as a possible diagnostic
signal of this bias. The full-information benchmark behaves as expected: its
surprise remains comparatively close to zero once the initial rounds have
passed. The accepts-only policy, in contrast, produces larger and more volatile
surprise, with positive values occurring particularly during the early rounds.
This is consistent with an overoptimistic historical performance estimate.
However, the absolute surprise does not increase monotonically with the
acceptance rounds, and its volatility prevents it from being interpreted as a
reliable quantitative measure of acceptance bias in the present setting. The
hypothesis is therefore only partially supported: surprise contains information
about the changing selection process, but its magnitude is not sufficiently
stable to serve as a standalone measure of acceptance bias.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, the simulation uses a
deliberately simple Gaussian DGP with a small number of observable and hidden
features. Second, the MNAR mechanism is represented by a specific overwrite rule
whose increasing contribution can make the accepts-only and full-information
policies more similar. Third, the realized surprise depends strongly on the
number of accepted bads. This motivated the use of a future window, which
reduces sampling variation but also reduces temporal resolution and requires a
stability assumption over the window. Excluding windows with very few accepted
bads also remove further observations from highly selective periods. Finally,
the analysis does not evaluate the performance of a specific RI method. The
results therefore provide evidence for a dynamic bias mechanism and for the
potential observability of its consequences, rather than an identified RI
procedure.

Future work can build on this framework in four directions. First, the
behavior of surprise could be studied more formally under a stable MAR process
to characterize its finite-sample variation and to distinguish genuine
selection-induced changes from ordinary estimation noise. Theoretical work could benefit
from the proposed measure theoretic characterization. For further simulation based research
probably other metrics besides AUROC and the KS statistic should be included that may be
less sensitive to highly imbalanced data. Second, the proposed framework can also work to study
evaluation methods developed for RI such as the Bayesian Evaluation framework
proposed by @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL, as other diagnostics signals of the acceptance induced
bias. Third, the dynamic formulation could be extended to more realistic
MNAR and manual-overwrite mechanisms and eventually connected to RI procedures
that use the observed dynamics explicitly.

The main contribution of this thesis is therefore not a new RI algorithm, but a
formulation of reject inference that makes the temporal feedback of selective
observation explicit and empirically testable. The numerical results indicate
that this feedback can progressively alter the accepted population and the
scorecards estimated from it, even when the underlying applicant population is
stationary. Surprise captures part of this effect, but the present analysis also
shows that observability is not equivalent to reliable measurement: a signal can
contain information about acceptance bias without providing a stable estimate
of its magnitude. This distinction provides the main point of departure for
future work on RI methods that use the dynamics of the acceptance process as an
additional source of information.
